passages.where: When the LORD asks what they have done, the man blames the woman whom God gave him, and the woman blames the serpent. The site's note says neither confesses plainly, and both end with the same two words, and I ate, the truth that sits at the bottom of every excuse. The plain note asks where we move the blame the same way.

After his sin with Bathsheba, David says he knows his transgressions and his sin is always before him. The site's plain note says his prayer has no but: not but she, not but the pressure, not but everyone does it. He names it and leans his whole weight on God's mercy.

Confronted by Samuel, Saul says I have sinned, and in the same breath asks Samuel to honor him before the elders of his people. The site's note on the chapter says that when first confronted he insisted he had obeyed and blamed the troops. An apology that asks to be seen well is still about the one apologizing.

After Jesus invites himself to his house, Zacchaeus stands and says he will give half his possessions to the poor and repay fourfold anyone he has cheated. The site's note says he answers the crowd's grumbling with deeds rather than argument, the practical repentance John the Baptist asked of tax collectors. The plain note says the welcome comes first, and then the repair follows, and it is real.

Jesus says that if you remember at the altar that your brother has something against you, leave your gift, go and be reconciled first, then come back. The site's note says worship waits for reconciliation. The plain note adds that this never means a person who has been harmed must go back to someone dangerous; making peace takes two.

The younger son rehearses a speech, I have sinned against heaven and against you, and plans to ask for a hired servant's place, but his father runs to him and never lets him finish. The site's plain note says the turning matters and the welcome is a gift. He came back asking for nothing he was owed.

He who conceals his sins will not prosper, but whoever confesses and renounces them will find mercy. The site's note calls this one of the Bible's clearest sayings on confession. Confessing and renouncing go together: naming the wrong, and turning from it.

Paul says godly sorrow brings repentance without regret, while worldly sorrow brings death, and describes the earnestness and eagerness to set things right that godly sorrow produced in the Corinthians. The site's plain note asks whether a person's sorrow was over what they had done, or over being found out. It adds that godly sorrow is meant to end in freedom, not to go on forever.

The law says that a person who wrongs another must confess the sin, make full restitution, add a fifth to its value, and give it to the one wronged. The site's note on the chapter sets this among the laws that protect the camp where God dwells. Confession in Israel was spoken and paid, not only felt.

James tells believers to confess their sins to each other and pray for each other, so that they may be healed. The site's plain note asks whether there is someone you need to confess to. A church is meant to be a place where wrong can be named without being hidden.

misread.taken: Against You, You only, have I sinned is used to say that an apology is owed to God alone, so that once a person has confessed in private prayer, nothing need be said to the one they hurt.
misread.says: The site's plain note says David is not saying that Bathsheba and Uriah were not harmed; in 2 Samuel 12 he accepts Nathan's charge about Uriah without arguing. Most readers take the verse to mean that every wrong done to a person is at its root also a wrong against God, who made that person and whose law protects them. None of these readings makes the harm smaller. They put it in front of God, and Jesus sends the one who remembers a wrong at the altar to go and be reconciled first.

whole: Most of us know how to apologize badly. I'm sorry you feel that way. I'm sorry, but you have to understand. Mistakes were made. I said I was sorry, what more do you want? Some people apologize all day for things that are not wrong, to keep the peace, and then find they cannot say it plainly when it matters. Others cannot say it at all, because admitting a wrong feels like losing the argument or losing face. Many families carry a wound that has lasted years because one sentence was never said.

Scripture knows the half apology from its first pages. When God asked what they had done, the man blamed the woman and, behind her, God who gave her; the woman blamed the serpent; and both ended with the same words, and I ate. Saul said I have sinned and in the next breath asked Samuel to honor him before the elders. The trouble with such apologies is not the words but that the speaker is still at the centre: protecting a name, managing the outcome, sharing out the blame. Paul names the difference as two kinds of sorrow, and the plain note puts the question simply: sorrow over what was done, or over being found out. Every one of us has given an apology like Saul's, and most of us have received one.

So the Bible's wisdom about apologizing is plain. Name the wrong without a but, as David's prayer does. Own it before the person, not only before God: Jesus says to leave the gift at the altar and go and be reconciled first. Make it right where it can be made right, as the law asked for full repayment and a fifth more, and Zacchaeus offered fourfold. Do not demand forgiveness or a quick return of trust; the son came home asking for a servant's place, not his rights. And confess to one another, as James says. Where the person you wronged is not safe to approach, or does not want contact, an apology may need to wait or come through someone else, and the site's note on Matthew 5 says making peace takes two.

The hope Scripture gives is that confession is met with mercy. Proverbs says whoever confesses and renounces his sins will find mercy, and John says God is faithful and just to forgive. The father in Jesus' story ran to his son before the speech was finished. That welcome is what makes an honest apology possible. A person who knows that God receives a broken and contrite heart no longer has to defend themselves so hard, and can say I was wrong, I am sorry, how can I make it right, and mean every word.
sit: Is there a sentence you owe someone, without a but, and what would it take to say it this week?

prayer.lead: The site's plain note says the psalm tells what silence costs and what confession gives, and notices how quickly God forgives in verse 5: I said, I will confess, and the next words are You forgave.
